title: DB-INR: Dual-Band Implicit Neural Representations for Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) fit a continuous coordinate network to an unlabeled test image and decode segmentation from its fitted features. We introduce DB-INR, a dual-band sinusoidal residual layer with independently initialized projections, a fixed equal mixture, scaled residual connections, and nearby frequency multipliers. Controlled ablations support these choices and show that learning a mixing gate provides no measurable benefit over a normalized fixed mixture. At matched parameter budgets, DB-INR achieves the highest mean Dice among the evaluated coordinate backbones on brain and cardiac MRI, with the cardiac margin within seed variability. It improves average performance across MedSegBench datasets and supports accurate decoding between fitting-grid samples. Label-free rigid alignment substantially improves robustness on template-normalized brain scans. Coordinate-prior probes identify limitations when anatomy is not consistently aligned.

figures.caption:
\textbf{Overview of the pipeline and of the DB-INR layer.} \textbf{(I)} A coordinate network $f_\theta$ and a per-pixel head $g_\phi$ are meta-learned with MAML under a reconstruction and a classification term. \textbf{(II)} At test time $f_\theta$ is fitted to an unseen scan with the reconstruction term alone and labels are read from its penultimate features in one pass, with $\phi$ frozen, so no annotation of the test scan is used. The block inside $f_{\theta^\star}$ is the DB-INR layer: a projection per band at its own effective frequency, the mixing gate pinned to the constant $\mathbf{g}=\tfrac12$ rather than learned, and a residual scaled by $1/\sqrt{2}$.}
\label{fig:pipeline
